records.focus: Old Havana and its Fortification System
records.hook: Cuba: Old Havana and its Fortification System

sections.title: A harbour that shaped a city
sections.body: Havana's old centre grew beside a sheltered bay that made the city important to Atlantic shipping. Its street plan still connects several distinct squares, each surrounded by buildings of different ages and purposes. The city was never simply a collection of grand facades: warehouses, houses with internal courtyards, workshops and waterfront defences all belonged to the same busy port economy.

sections.title: Trade, empire and defensive walls
sections.body: Spanish colonial authorities developed Havana as a strategic stop for ships crossing the Atlantic. The fortifications guarding the narrow entrance to the bay reveal how much effort went into controlling that movement. Across the historic centre, Baroque and neoclassical details stand beside more modest arcaded homes. The contrast helps explain how maritime wealth, military priorities and everyday urban life became physically intertwined.

sections.title: A living city, not a preserved set
sections.body: Old Havana remains a place where people live, work and negotiate the demands of maintaining ageing buildings. Restoration cannot be judged only by whether a facade looks freshly painted: the condition of housing, public spaces and local services matters too. Hurricanes and salt-laden coastal weather add pressure to structures already shaped by centuries of adaptation. Heritage management therefore has a social as well as architectural dimension.

sections.title: What to notice on the map
sections.body: Follow the line between the waterfront, the old squares and the forts rather than treating them as separate attractions. The harbour explains why the defences occupy particular positions; the plazas explain how public life developed inland. A useful surprise is that Havana's celebrated architecture is inseparable from ordinary courtyards and streets. This heritage focus is in Havana, not at every point in Cuba.

records.quickFact: Follow the line between the waterfront, the old squares and the forts rather than treating them as separate attractions.

records.hook: Dominican Republic: Colonial City of Santo Domingo

sections.title: A city at the mouth of a river
sections.body: The historic centre of Santo Domingo stands beside the Ozama River on the southern coast of Hispaniola. Its position helped connect the island to maritime routes and to the expanding Spanish colonial administration. Streets, civic buildings and religious institutions were planned together, giving the settlement an unusually influential early urban layout. That grid is still legible beneath centuries of subsequent change.

sections.title: An influential but unequal beginning
sections.body: Santo Domingo became an early centre of European colonial government in the Americas. Its cathedral, hospital and other institutions are often described as regional firsts, but that language should not obscure the conquest and exploitation accompanying colonial expansion. The surviving buildings tell a history of political authority as well as craftsmanship. Understanding both sides gives the architecture a more accurate context than a simple celebration of age.

sections.title: How the city kept changing
sections.body: The old quarter was not frozen when its original walls and streets were built. Houses were altered, businesses occupied older structures, and public spaces took on new uses. Conservation today has to balance the value of stonework and street patterns with the needs of residents. The Ozama's waterfront setting also makes it clear why the settlement was placed here rather than farther inland.

sections.title: Read the streets as evidence
sections.body: Look for the repeated blocks of the street grid, then compare them with the river's irregular edge. This contrast reveals how an imposed plan met a real landscape. Fortified structures and civic buildings show which activities colonial rulers considered important. The site is in Santo Domingo itself; it is one historical focus within the Dominican Republic, not a description of every community on Hispaniola.

records.hook: Jamaica: Blue and John Crow Mountains

sections.title: Two ranges with many habitats
sections.body: Eastern Jamaica's Blue and John Crow Mountains rise sharply from surrounding lowlands, creating changes in rainfall, temperature and vegetation over short distances. High ridges support cloud-influenced forests where mosses, ferns and orchids grow among twisted trees. The mountains are part of a wider living landscape, not an empty green backdrop. Their difficult terrain has shaped both ecology and human history.

sections.title: Refuge, resistance and memory
sections.body: The mountains provided refuge for Indigenous Taíno people and later for Maroon communities resisting enslavement and colonial control. Routes, settlements and remembered places are associated with survival and organised resistance. These connections remain important to cultural identity and living traditions. A description limited to mountain scenery would miss why UNESCO recognises this as cultural as well as natural heritage.

sections.title: Species found in few other places
sections.body: Isolation and differences in elevation have helped produce a striking concentration of plants found only in Jamaica or in even smaller parts of the mountain region. Birds, frogs and other wildlife depend on specialised habitats. Forest protection matters because clearing or fragmenting a small area can affect species with very restricted ranges. Cultural knowledge and biodiversity conservation are both part of the area's significance.

sections.title: Look beyond the highest summit
sections.body: The steep slopes, hidden valleys and changes in forest height are more revealing than a single viewpoint. Consider how a route through the mountains could have offered both protection and difficulty to people moving through it. The heritage landscape lies in eastern Jamaica; it does not represent every Jamaican environment. Its unusual distinction is the close connection between ecological refuge and histories of freedom.

records.quickFact: The steep slopes, hidden valleys and changes in forest height are more revealing than a single viewpoint.

records.hook: Dominica: Morne Trois Pitons National Park

sections.title: A volcanic interior
sections.body: Dominica's mountainous interior is shaped by volcanic activity and heavy tropical rainfall. Morne Trois Pitons National Park protects steep ridges, deep valleys and a range of hot-water and steam features. These are signs of an active geological setting rather than decorative curiosities. Dense forest covers much of the landscape, creating an environment where weather, water and rock are constantly interacting.

sections.title: Heat beneath a wet forest
sections.body: Hot springs, fumaroles and the famous Boiling Lake demonstrate that heat from below ground can be visible at the surface. Elsewhere, rivers and waterfalls cut through the slopes. The combination is unusual: visitors encounter geothermal activity within a very wet, heavily vegetated island landscape. The precise conditions around hot-water features can change, so they should be understood as protected natural systems, not casual swimming spots.

sections.title: Habitats under pressure
sections.body: The park's different elevations and valleys support varied plant and animal communities. Tropical storms, invasive species and human pressure can affect forests and waterways, while recovery may take time. Conservation is therefore about the functioning of connected habitats, not simply keeping a boundary on a map. Dominica's wider communities and landscapes also extend far beyond the national park.

sections.title: A useful geographical distinction
sections.body: Dominica is a separate Caribbean country from the Dominican Republic, despite the similar names. Its Morne Trois Pitons heritage focus is inland, not on a capital-city waterfront. On the map, look at the way short distances separate coast, rainforest and high volcanic terrain. That compact variation helps explain the island's remarkable natural diversity and the need for careful protection.

records.quickFact: Dominica is a separate Caribbean country from the Dominican Republic, despite the similar names.

sections.title: A walled city facing the Adriatic
sections.body: Dubrovnik occupies a dramatic position on Croatia's southern Adriatic coast. Its walls, streets and harbour make sense together: maritime trade helped sustain a city that also needed protection from attack and political pressure. The compact historic centre contains public buildings, homes and religious architecture from several periods. The walls are a working clue to the city's history, not merely a scenic outline.

sections.title: Maritime power and civic life
sections.body: From the medieval period, Dubrovnik developed as an important Mediterranean trading centre. Its urban fabric reflects a long tradition of administration, commerce and negotiation with stronger neighbouring powers. Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque elements can be seen in buildings that survived or were rebuilt after damage. The great earthquake of 1667 is an important reminder that the city visible today reflects reconstruction as well as continuity.

sections.title: Damage and careful repair
sections.body: The historic centre was damaged during armed conflict in the 1990s, adding another difficult chapter to its conservation history. Repairing masonry is only one part of preserving a city whose streets also support residents, services and tourism. Heavy visitor numbers can change how public space is used. The challenge is to keep the old centre a functioning urban neighbourhood while respecting its exceptional fabric.

sections.title: Read the shape of the city
sections.body: Notice how the harbour, walls and street pattern respond to the rocky coastline. The view from above can make Dubrovnik appear almost self-contained, yet its prosperity depended on connections across the sea. This heritage site is in Dubrovnik, not in Croatia's capital Zagreb. The surprising story is how a small coastal city repeatedly adapted to trade, disaster and changing political conditions.

sections.title: A meeting place in a rift landscape
sections.body: Þingvellir lies in a dramatic valley marked by geological fractures. Its open ground and steep rocky edges became the setting for the Alþing, an assembly established around 930. The place brings political history into direct contact with a visibly changing landscape. It is not simply a parliament building without walls: the meeting place extended across an outdoor area used for gathering, discussion and legal decisions.

sections.title: Law, assembly and society
sections.body: For centuries people travelled to the assembly to settle disputes, hear laws and conduct business. The surviving remains include traces of temporary booths made from turf and stone. These modest structures are as informative as grand monuments because they show how the gathering worked in practice. The assembly's history is central to Icelandic cultural memory, although its early society was not equally inclusive for everyone.

sections.title: Geology beside human history
sections.body: The fissures and cliffs are part of Iceland's tectonic setting, where the land is being pulled apart. Water, vegetation and exposed rock give the valley its distinctive appearance. Archaeological remains are vulnerable within that environment, so managing foot traffic and preserving the ground itself are important. The landscape is both a geological attraction and an archive of how people used a particular place over many generations.

sections.title: A detail easy to miss
sections.body: Look for low archaeological traces rather than expecting a huge surviving hall. The open-air assembly relied on people gathering in a landscape, and much of its material evidence is subtle. Þingvellir is east of Reykjavík, not within the capital. Its importance comes from the unusually clear relationship between a long-lived political institution and the physical setting where it met.

records.quickFact: Look for low archaeological traces rather than expecting a huge surviving hall.

sections.title: Where a great river slows down
sections.body: After crossing much of Europe, the Danube reaches the Black Sea through a branching wetland landscape. Sediment, channels, lakes and reed beds form a shifting delta rather than a fixed river mouth. Water levels and seasonal movements influence where plants grow and where birds feed. The scale of the marshes is one reason this landscape matters far beyond Romania's coast.

sections.title: Birds, fish and changing water
sections.body: The delta supports large numbers of bird species, including birds that use it during migration, as well as many freshwater fish. Different habitats lie close together: open water, reed beds, floating vegetation and patches of higher ground. Their connections matter because an alteration to water flow in one place can affect feeding or breeding conditions elsewhere. Protecting individual species means protecting the wider wetland system.

sections.title: People in a working landscape
sections.body: Communities have lived and worked around the delta's waterways, using boats and adapting to a geography in which water often determines access. Fishing, transport and tourism coexist with conservation rules. The area also receives the effects of activities farther upstream in the Danube basin. That makes its future partly dependent on decisions taken well beyond the protected area's boundaries.

sections.title: Follow the channels, not one pin
sections.body: A single map marker cannot show the delta's many branches. Look at the way the river separates into channels before meeting the Black Sea, and imagine how a flood or a change in sediment supply might alter the pattern. The heritage focus is in eastern Romania, not Bucharest. Its distinctive feature is the close link between continental river processes and an internationally important wetland.

records.quickFact: A single map marker cannot show the delta's many branches.

sections.title: A wooded hill landscape near the ocean
sections.body: Sintra rises in wooded hills west of Lisbon, close enough to the Atlantic for its climate to differ from hotter inland areas. Palaces, gardens, old religious buildings and country houses occupy a landscape shaped deliberately over many centuries. The hills and vegetation are not just scenery behind the architecture. They are part of the heritage itself and help explain why the place attracted successive patrons.

sections.title: Romanticism built into the terrain
sections.body: In the nineteenth century, Ferdinand II transformed a former monastery into the colourful Pena Palace and developed surrounding parkland. Designers mixed architectural references and planted both local and imported species. The result reflects European Romantic ideas about history, nature and imagination. Sintra is therefore different from a single castle preserved in isolation: paths, planted vistas and buildings were conceived as an experience.

sections.title: Older layers beneath the gardens
sections.body: The landscape contains traces of earlier periods, including the Moorish Castle and historic royal buildings. The nineteenth-century transformation did not erase those layers; it often reinterpreted them. That mixture makes the area valuable but also complicated to maintain. Gardens need care, trees grow or die, and historic structures face the effects of moisture and heavy visitation. Conservation here involves living vegetation as well as masonry.

sections.title: Look for planned surprises
sections.body: A bend in a path may reveal a tower, a distant view or an unexpected planting. These moments were often designed, rather than discovered by accident. Sintra is not in central Lisbon, even though it is frequently visited from the capital. The unusual lesson is that a whole landscape can be an artwork while still carrying older histories and functioning as a real place.

records.focus: Jiuzhaigou Valley Scenic and Historic Interest Area
records.hook: China: Jiuzhaigou Valley Scenic and Historic Interest Area

sections.title: Mountain valleys and coloured water
sections.body: Jiuzhaigou lies in the mountains of northern Sichuan, far from China's major coastal cities. Its forests, waterfalls and clear lakes occupy a steep valley system shaped by geology and flowing water. Mineral-rich conditions and the way light passes through water help produce striking colours, but the lakes are living parts of a connected landscape. Their appearance changes with seasons, weather and water levels.

sections.title: Many habitats in one protected area
sections.body: The altitude range supports different forest communities, from lower mountain vegetation to colder high-elevation habitats. The wider region is associated with rare wildlife, including the giant panda and Sichuan takin, though sightings are never guaranteed. Birds and plants form a much larger part of the ecological story than any single famous animal. Protecting the valley means maintaining the water systems and forests together.

sections.title: People, place and conservation
sections.body: The scenic area sits within a region with Tibetan cultural connections and inhabited landscapes. Tourism brings attention and income but also pressure on paths, transport and sensitive waters. Natural disturbances can reshape steep mountain terrain, so management has to respond to environmental change rather than promise an unchanging postcard view. Respect for local communities belongs alongside the protection of wildlife and scenery.

sections.title: What the map cannot show
sections.body: The valley is a long landscape, not one lake at a single point. Follow the branching terrain and consider how water moving downhill links pools, waterfalls and forests. Jiuzhaigou is in Sichuan, not Beijing, and the heritage description should not be confused with a general account of all China. Its special interest is the meeting of altitude, water chemistry and mountain ecology.

records.quickFact: The valley is a long landscape, not one lake at a single point.

sections.title: A landscape of cities and water
sections.body: Angkor in north-western Cambodia covers far more ground than the famous towers of Angkor Wat. Across a broad landscape lie temples, roads, reservoirs, canals and traces of successive Khmer capitals. The scale of the water-management system is especially revealing: settlement and farming depended on organising water as well as constructing monumental religious buildings. Forest and inhabited areas remain part of the setting.

sections.title: Art and political history
sections.body: From the ninth to the fifteenth centuries, Khmer rulers built religious and civic complexes that changed over time. Angkor Wat, the Bayon and other monuments show different artistic approaches and religious associations. Their stone carvings are historical evidence as well as decoration. Understanding the site requires looking at several periods, not imagining a single king or one short moment of construction.

sections.title: A place where people still live
sections.body: Villages and agricultural land exist within the wider archaeological park, and local communities maintain cultural connections with its temples and landscapes. Conservation therefore cannot treat the area as an abandoned museum. Visitor pressure, infrastructure and environmental conditions all affect the monuments. Careful management must consider the livelihoods of residents alongside the physical survival of ancient buildings and water structures.

sections.title: Find the hidden engineering
sections.body: On a map, look beyond the most recognisable temple to the long reservoirs and canals that connect the former urban landscape. Their size helps explain how extensive the Khmer capitals became. Angkor is near Siem Reap, not in Phnom Penh, Cambodia's present capital. A memorable detail is that some of the site's most consequential architecture was built to manage water rather than to be admired.

records.quickFact: On a map, look beyond the most recognisable temple to the long reservoirs and canals that connect the former urban landscape.

records.hook: Sri Lanka: Ancient City of Sigiriya

sections.title: A fortress above the plains
sections.body: Sigiriya rises abruptly from the surrounding lowlands of central Sri Lanka. The rock's steep sides made it a dramatic location for a royal complex associated with King Kassapa in the fifth century. Ruins occupy the summit and the ground below. The setting helps explain both the site's defensive possibilities and its visual impact: a relatively compact formation dominates the landscape around it.

sections.title: Art, gardens and royal ambition
sections.body: The complex includes traces of designed gardens, water features, walls and painted surfaces, not only the remains at the top of the rock. Access routes once passed a monumental lion-shaped entrance, giving the site its familiar name, Lion Rock. These elements suggest a carefully planned royal environment. They also show how architecture, art and landscape were used together to project authority.

sections.title: A fragile archaeological record
sections.body: Weathering, vegetation and heavy foot traffic can affect ancient surfaces and structures. Preserving the site means looking after the less obvious evidence on lower terraces as well as the famous elevated remains. The surrounding environment is part of the archaeological story because the rock's position made the complex possible. Visitors see only a fraction of the work involved in studying and maintaining it.

sections.title: Notice the route as much as the view
sections.body: The ascent makes the height of the rock obvious, but the route itself reveals how movement through the complex was controlled. Compare the water gardens below with the remains above to understand the site's planned organisation. Sigiriya is not in Colombo, Sri Lanka's commercial capital. Its surprising feature is the combination of a spectacular natural outcrop with a highly designed human landscape.

records.quickFact: The ascent makes the height of the rock obvious, but the route itself reveals how movement through the complex was controlled.

sections.title: An oasis on long-distance routes
sections.body: Samarkand developed in the Zerafshan valley, where access to water and connections across Central Asia helped sustain a major urban centre. Its history extends well before the monuments most visitors recognise. Traders, scholars and craftspeople moved through the region, bringing ideas and skills as well as goods. The city's identity as a crossroads is rooted in geography and repeated cultural exchange.

sections.title: The Timurid architectural legacy
sections.body: Samarkand flourished as a political and artistic centre under the Timurids in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The Registan's madrasas, the Bibi-Khanum Mosque and the Shah-i-Zinda complex display ambitious design and intricate decoration. Their scale can distract from the work of builders, tile makers and scholars whose knowledge made such projects possible. These monuments represent one especially visible layer of a much longer urban history.

sections.title: Science and everyday life
sections.body: Ulugh Beg's observatory connects Samarkand to the history of astronomical observation and mathematical study. Religious education, markets and neighbourhood life also shaped the city. Conservation has to consider how old structures fit into a modern settlement, not just how their surfaces appear in photographs. The historic area includes archaeological remains and later buildings whose relationships help explain change over time.

sections.title: Look for more than blue domes
sections.body: The striking tilework is worth examining, but the placement of squares, schools and routes tells a larger story about the city's role. Samarkand is not Uzbekistan's capital, Tashkent. Its heritage value comes from several interacting periods and traditions, with the Timurid monuments offering a particularly visible chapter rather than the whole history of the region.

records.quickFact: The striking tilework is worth examining, but the placement of squares, schools and routes tells a larger story about the city's role.
